greek.meaning: spirited passion, courage, anger, the seat of emotion and will
greek.forms: nominative θυμός, genitive θυμοῦ, dative θυμῷ, accusative θυμόν
greek.etymology: From Proto-Indo-European *dʰewh₂- (to smoke, fume). Related to θύω (to rage, rush) and originally connected to the breath or vital spirit rising from the chest.
greek.literary_context: Homer uses θυμός throughout the Iliad to describe the passionate, spirited part of the hero's psyche, as when Achilles debates in his θυμός whether to kill Agamemnon (Iliad 1.188-192). Plato later distinguishes θυμός as the spirited part of the tripartite soul in Republic Book 4.
greek.usage_example: μένος καὶ θυμὸν ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν ἔχοντες. — Having might and spirited courage in their breasts.
greek.did_you_know: The θυμός was originally conceived as a physical organ located in the chest, the source of breath and passionate feeling, distinct from both rational νοῦς and physical ψυχή. Its semantic range spans from heroic valor to wrathful anger, making it central to understanding Homeric psychology.

latin.meaning: in vain, to no purpose, without effect
latin.forms: indeclinable adverb; related to frustrātiō (deception, disappointment) and frustrō (deceive, disappoint)
latin.etymology: From *fraud-tro-, cognate with fraus (fraud, deceit); the root sense involves being cheated or deceived, hence producing no result. The semantic development moved from 'by fraud' to 'ineffectually.'
latin.literary_context: Virgil uses frūstrā repeatedly in the Aeneid to mark futile efforts: Dido's attempt to detain Aeneas, Turnus's resistance to fate, and Priam's final stand against Pyrrhus all occur frūstrā, emphasizing the tragic inevitability of divine will.
latin.usage_example: Frūstrā magnus Priamus tēla gerit. — Great Priam bears arms in vain.
latin.did_you_know: The word appears at dramatically charged moments in epic poetry to signal that human effort, however heroic, cannot alter predetermined outcomes. Lucretius also employs it when describing the futile fear of death that haunts mortals who fail to grasp Epicurean philosophy.

french.meaning: to undulate, to ripple, to wave gently (like water or fabric)
french.forms: Present: j'ondoie, tu ondoies, il ondoie, nous ondoyons, vous ondoyez, ils ondoient. Past participle: ondoyé. Imperfect: j'ondoyais.
french.etymology: From Latin unda (wave), through the verb form undulare. The French ondoyer preserves the Latin root with typical phonetic evolution: unda > onde, with the verb suffix -oyer.
french.literary_context: Mallarmé uses ondoyer in his poems to evoke the sinuous movement of hair and veils, as in L'Après-midi d'un faune where the faun describes nymphs whose hair undulates in the breeze. Hugo employs it in Les Contemplations to describe waves and shifting light.
french.usage_example: Les blés ondoyaient sous le vent de juin. — The wheat fields rippled under the June wind.
french.did_you_know: In ecclesiastical French, ondoyer also means to perform emergency baptism by sprinkling water, derived from the same root. Baudelaire favored this verb for its liquid musicality when describing feminine movement and natural phenomena.

german.forms: das Heimweh, gen. des Heimwehs (no plural in this sense)
german.etymology: From Middle High German heimwē, compound of heim 'home' (cognate with English 'home') + wē 'pain, woe' (related to English 'woe'). The literal sense is 'home-pain' or 'pain for home.'
german.literary_context: Hölderlin employs Heimweh extensively in his late hymns, particularly in 'Brot und Wein,' where the poet expresses longing for ancient Greece and the lost divine presence in the modern world.
german.usage_example: Das Heimweh nach der verlorenen Heimat quälte ihn sein ganzes Leben. — The homesickness for his lost homeland tormented him his entire life.
german.did_you_know: The Swiss recognized Heimweh as a serious medical condition in the 17th century, sometimes called 'Swiss disease,' affecting mercenaries far from their mountain homes; physicians believed it could prove fatal if untreated.

italian.etymology: From Latin vēltrārius or vēltrus, possibly of Celtic origin, related to hunting dogs. The word appears in medieval Latin as veltrum.
italian.literary_context: Dante prophesies in Inferno I.101-111 that a veltro will come to chase the she-wolf (representing greed) back to Hell, bringing salvation to Italy. This mysterious greyhound has inspired centuries of allegorical interpretation.
italian.usage_example: Questi non ciberà terra né peltro, / ma sapïenza, amore e virtute. — This one will not feed on land or pewter, but on wisdom, love, and virtue.
italian.did_you_know: The identity of Dante's veltro remains one of the great puzzles of the Commedia. Scholars have proposed it represents Can Grande della Scala (whose name means great dog), a future emperor, Christ himself, or an ideal political redeemer who never came.

oldenglish.meaning: accursed warrior; outlaw branded for killing; one condemned for violence
oldenglish.forms: nom. sg. heoruwearh; gen. sg. heoruwearges; nom. pl. heoruweargas; dat. pl. heoruwearġum
oldenglish.etymology: Compound of heoru 'sword, battle' (from Proto-Germanic *heruz) + wearh 'criminal, outcast, wolf' (related to Gothic wargjan 'to condemn'). The second element shares ancestry with Latin vargus and carries connotations of one placed outside social protection.
oldenglish.literary_context: The word appears in Beowulf (line 1267) to describe Grendel, marking him as both a warrior-figure and a creature fundamentally cursed and excluded from the hall-society of men.
oldenglish.usage_example: Sē heoruwearh hēt healreced sēcan. — The accursed warrior commanded to seek the hall-building.
oldenglish.did_you_know: The wearh element originally meant 'wolf' in Germanic languages, reflecting the practice of declaring criminals as literal outlaws who could be hunted like wolves, a status called wulfshēafod in Old English law codes.

middleenglish.meaning: power, dominion, control; aloofness, disdain; peril
middleenglish.forms: singular: daunger; plural: daungers (rare in abstract sense)
middleenglish.etymology: From Old French dangier, from Vulgar Latin *dominārium (power of a lord), from Latin dominium (lordship, ownership), from dominus (lord, master). The semantic shift from 'lordship' to 'aloofness' to 'peril' reflects medieval social hierarchy.
middleenglish.literary_context: In the Roman de la Rose tradition and Chaucer's Romaunt of the Rose, Daunger personified is the allegorical guardian who keeps lovers at a distance through haughty refusal. Chaucer uses the word frequently in Troilus and Criseyde to describe both the beloved's standoffishness and actual peril.
middleenglish.usage_example: She held him longe in daunger and desdayn, er she graunted him hire love. — She held him long in aloof disdain before she granted him her love.
middleenglish.did_you_know: The modern sense of physical peril emerged only gradually in Middle English; the earlier dominant meaning was the power someone held over you, especially a lady's dismissive control over her suitor in courtly love literature.

welsh.meaning: chief yellow; primrose; also used as a proper name
welsh.forms: plural: cynfelynnau. In Middle Welsh appears as cynuelyn, kynuelyn
welsh.etymology: From cyn- 'chief, first' + melyn 'yellow'. The flower name derives from its being the first or chief yellow flower of spring. The personal name Cynfelyn (Latin Cunobelinus) contains the same British Celtic elements *kuno- 'high, chief' + *belino- 'bright'.
welsh.literary_context: The word appears in the medieval plant lists and herbals. Dafydd ap Gwilym uses floral imagery extensively in his cywyddau, though he more commonly employs other spring flowers like the lily and rose to praise his beloveds.
welsh.usage_example: Yn y gwanwyn daw'r cynfelyn i flodeuo yn y perthi. — In spring the primrose comes to bloom in the hedgerows.
welsh.did_you_know: The historical British king Cunobelinus (died c. 40 AD), whose name became Cynfelyn in Welsh tradition, was Shakespeare's Cymbeline. The name literally means 'chief bright one' or 'hound of Belenus', connecting royal nomenclature to both solar imagery and the ancient Celtic god of light.

oldnorse.meaning: sage, wise man, reciter of sacred lore
oldnorse.forms: nom. sg. þulr, acc. þul, gen. þuls, dat. þuli; nom. pl. þular
oldnorse.etymology: From Proto-Norse *þulaz, related to Old English þyle 'orator, spokesman' and Gothic þul-s in proper names. Root likely Proto-Germanic *þul-ǭ- 'speak solemnly,' possibly from PIE *teu-l- 'swell,' extended to mean 'speak with elevated authority.'
oldnorse.literary_context: In Hávamál stanza 80, Odin refers to himself as þulr when seated on the high seat (hásæti) delivering wisdom. The term also appears in Snorri's Prose Edda as a title for court sages who preserved genealogies and mythic knowledge through oral recitation.
oldnorse.usage_example: Hann var kallaðr þulr konungs, því at hann kunni margar fornar sǫgur. — He was called the king's sage, because he knew many ancient tales.
oldnorse.did_you_know: The þulr held an official position in pre-Christian Scandinavian courts, sitting in a designated seat during feasts to recite þulur (ritual name-lists) and genealogies. This practice preserved oral tradition before the arrival of writing, making the þulr a living repository of cultural memory.
